conversations.title: Which component is failing?
conversations.setting: An engineer and a product manager inspect an incorrect answer from a document assistant.
turns: Product manager
The AI gave the wrong answer. Should we replace the model?
Engineer
First, let's separate retrieval, answer generation, and what the interface displays.
Product manager
The displayed answer refers to last year's handbook. Which layer controls that?
Engineer
Retrieval supplies passages. The language model uses them to draft an answer.
Product manager
So an old passage could produce an answer that sounds current?
Engineer
Yes. We need the retrieved passages before attributing this example to the model.
Product manager
The trace shows last year's handbook among the returned documents.
Engineer
Then let's inspect document versioning and retrieval before changing the foundation model.
Product manager
I'll attach the question, displayed answer, and document version to the issue.
Engineer
Good. I'll trace that request and distinguish confirmed findings from possible causes.

conversations.title: A queue is not a slow model
conversations.setting: A serving engineer explains response timing to a new colleague.
turns: Colleague
Users waited twelve seconds, but the inference log records only four.
Serving engineer
The request also spent eight seconds waiting in the serving queue.
Colleague
Does inference mean the entire period from clicking Send to seeing an answer?
Serving engineer
Here, inference means running the model. End-to-end latency includes the other stages.
Colleague
Then our dashboard label is making two different measures look interchangeable.
Serving engineer
Exactly. Let's label queue time, model execution, and total response time separately.
Colleague
Would increasing throughput mean every individual request becomes faster?
Serving engineer
Not necessarily. Throughput measures completed work per period, not one request's duration.
Colleague
I'll revise the labels and include both measures in the incident summary.
Serving engineer
Include the measurement boundaries too, so the next comparison uses the same definition.

conversations.title: One answer, two displays
conversations.setting: A frontend developer and an AI engineer investigate a missing citation.
turns: Frontend developer
The answer on screen has no citation, so retrieval must have failed.
AI engineer
Let's check the response payload before drawing that conclusion.
Frontend developer
The payload contains a passage identifier and a citation URL.
AI engineer
Then the backend returned citation information. The display may be dropping it.
Frontend developer
The new interface expects a citations array, but this response uses source.
AI engineer
That looks like a contract mismatch between the service and the interface.
Frontend developer
I'll reproduce it with a saved response rather than another live model call.
AI engineer
Good. That isolates rendering from retrieval and generation variability.
Frontend developer
Once the mapping is fixed, should we also test empty citation lists?
AI engineer
Yes. Check both cases and avoid treating missing evidence as a display-only problem.

additional_scenario.title: The spinner stays on
additional_scenario.brief: The model service has returned an answer, but the interface still displays a loading indicator. A trace contains a successful service response; the frontend event log has not been checked.
additional_scenario.role_a: You are the AI engineer. Explain the difference between completed inference and a completed user interaction.
additional_scenario.role_b: You are the frontend developer. Ask which evidence is available and what you should inspect next.
additional_scenario.opening_line: The model returned an answer, but we haven't established why the interface is still waiting.
additional_scenario.complication: The product manager asks you to describe the issue without using the words inference or payload.
success_checks: Distinguish the service response from the interface state.
Do not claim the frontend cause is confirmed.
Agree which log or event to inspect next.

conversations.title: More output space will not fit the input
conversations.setting: Two engineers review a request rejected for exceeding the model's context limit.
turns: Developer
The request is too long. Could we just increase the output allowance?
AI engineer
That won't shorten the prompt or the retrieved documents already in the request.
Developer
I thought the context window meant the answer's maximum length.
AI engineer
It is the model's available context, not simply the number of answer tokens.
Developer
Our application reserves answer space before adding retrieved passages.
AI engineer
Then we should inspect that budget and count the assembled request.
Developer
Could I delete the oldest conversation messages until it fits?
AI engineer
Only after checking whether they contain constraints the current question still needs.
Developer
I'll measure each part and propose a documented truncation rule.
AI engineer
Test that rule on follow-up questions, not only standalone prompts.

conversations.title: The token count changed
conversations.setting: A localization lead compares English and Japanese requests in the team's test environment.
turns: Localization lead
Both requests have about the same character count. Why do their token counts differ?
Engineer
The tokenizer doesn't assign exactly one token to each character or word.
Localization lead
Can I use the English average to estimate the Japanese requests?
Engineer
We should measure those requests with the tokenizer used by our deployed model.
Localization lead
The Japanese sample includes product codes and mixed punctuation as well.
Engineer
Include those in the test set. They are part of our actual input.
Localization lead
Would a word limit in the interface still protect the context budget?
Engineer
It would be an approximation, not a guarantee that the assembled request fits.
Localization lead
I'll collect representative samples and flag the largest assembled requests.
Engineer
I'll report token counts by sample and keep the tokenizer version in the results.

conversations.title: Instructions and quoted text
conversations.setting: A prompt designer and reviewer discuss a document summarization request.
turns: Reviewer
This quoted document tells the assistant to ignore the requested output format.
Prompt designer
That sentence is document content, not an instruction we intend to authorize.
Reviewer
Is placing our format rule in the system prompt sufficient proof of protection?
Prompt designer
No. We still need to test whether the assistant follows the intended boundary.
Reviewer
Let's include documents that contain instruction-like language in the evaluation.
Prompt designer
Agreed. I'll keep document text clearly delimited in the request structure.
Reviewer
Should the summary mention the instruction-like sentence if it is relevant?
Prompt designer
It may describe the sentence as content without treating it as a command.
Reviewer
I'll check both the output format and whether any unauthorized action occurred.
Prompt designer
Record the full test conditions so a passing example doesn't become a blanket claim.

additional_scenario.title: What can be shortened?
additional_scenario.brief: A test request is over the application's token budget. It contains a mandatory output schema, three repeated examples, and six retrieved passages. Relevance has not yet been assessed.
additional_scenario.role_a: You maintain the prompt. Propose an order for reviewing redundant or irrelevant content.
additional_scenario.role_b: You own the evaluation. Ask how the proposed shortening could affect correctness and follow-up questions.
additional_scenario.opening_line: Before removing constraints, let's check repeated examples and passage relevance.
additional_scenario.complication: A colleague wants to remove the output schema because it is the longest single instruction.
success_checks: Separate mandatory constraints from potentially redundant context.
Ask for relevance evidence rather than guessing which passage is unnecessary.
Propose a comparison using the same test questions.

conversations.title: The ninety-four percent result
conversations.setting: An evaluation owner briefs a release lead before a meeting.
turns: Release lead
Can I present the ninety-four percent score as evidence that we're ready?
Evaluation owner
Not without a caveat. Some evaluation examples also occur in training data.
Release lead
Does that mean every answer in the evaluation is invalid?
Evaluation owner
No, but the overlap compromises the independence of the reported evaluation.
Release lead
Can you calculate a clean score before the meeting in an hour?
Evaluation owner
I can identify known overlaps. I can't promise a completed independent rerun yet.
Release lead
Then what should the slide say about the current pass rate?
Evaluation owner
Label it provisional and state that training-evaluation overlap was detected.
Release lead
I'll separate the current result from any claim about unseen examples.
Evaluation owner
I'll bring the overlap evidence and the proposed replacement evaluation plan.

conversations.title: Duplicates with different filenames
conversations.setting: A data engineer and evaluator examine two apparently separate dataset partitions.
turns: Evaluator
The file identifiers differ, so I assumed these examples were independent.
Data engineer
The underlying text can still be duplicated even when identifiers change.
Evaluator
This question has different punctuation but the same reference answer.
Data engineer
Let's check exact duplicates and near-duplicates, and record how we identify each.
Evaluator
Should we remove every example that discusses the same subject?
Data engineer
Shared subject matter isn't automatically duplication. We need a defensible matching rule.
Evaluator
I'll review borderline matches rather than silently deleting them.
Data engineer
Keep the original split and the filtered version so the change is auditable.
Evaluator
The report will show the rule, removed counts, and remaining evaluation size.
Data engineer
Good. Don't compare the new percentage with the old one without explaining the changed set.

conversations.title: Disagreement in the golden set
conversations.setting: Two annotators and their lead discuss conflicting labels on a support-answer benchmark.
turns: Annotator
We disagree on this answer. I marked it correct because the main fact is right.
Annotation lead
What did the other labeler identify as the error?
Annotator
The answer omits a required condition from the reference policy.
Annotation lead
Does our rubric say whether that omission changes the correctness label?
Annotator
It says complete, but it doesn't define which details are essential.
Annotation lead
Then resolve the rubric ambiguity before treating either label as authoritative.
Annotator
Should we send the model's response back through training immediately?
Annotation lead
No. First record the adjudication and preserve the evaluation boundary.
Annotator
I'll draft a specific rule and bring comparable examples for review.
Annotation lead
Then recheck affected labels consistently and version the golden set.

additional_scenario.title: A benchmark used as a tutorial
additional_scenario.brief: A developer pasted five evaluation questions into a team prompt tutorial. You do not yet know whether the tutorial examples were later included in fine-tuning data.
additional_scenario.role_a: You own the benchmark. Explain the possible contamination and request provenance information.
additional_scenario.role_b: You manage training data. Distinguish known reuse from unconfirmed inclusion in a training run.
additional_scenario.opening_line: The questions were reused in a tutorial, but we haven't traced whether they reached training.
additional_scenario.complication: The release lead asks you to call the benchmark clean because no matching filename was found.
success_checks: State what reuse is confirmed.
Avoid equating a missing filename match with evidence of independence.
Agree how to trace content and qualify the current score.

conversations.title: Relevance versus response time
conversations.setting: A retrieval engineer presents a reranking experiment to a product manager.
turns: Product manager
The reranker finds better passages. Can we announce a better user experience?
Retrieval engineer
We measured passage relevance, not user experience. It also adds three hundred milliseconds.
Product manager
Is that enough delay for users to notice?
Retrieval engineer
We haven't run a user study, so I wouldn't claim either way.
Product manager
Then how should we describe the benefit in the experiment summary?
Retrieval engineer
Higher measured retrieval relevance, with additional response time in this test.
Product manager
Could we compare answers with and without reranking on the same questions?
Retrieval engineer
Yes. That would help establish whether the better passages improve answer quality.
Product manager
Let's include the latency distribution as well as the average.
Retrieval engineer
I'll keep the query set fixed and document the comparison conditions.

conversations.title: Similar is not necessarily relevant
conversations.setting: A support specialist asks why vector search returned an unhelpful passage.
turns: Support specialist
This passage mentions refunds repeatedly, but it doesn't answer the deadline question.
Search engineer
Semantic similarity alone doesn't guarantee that a passage contains the required detail.
Support specialist
Would asking for more results solve the problem?
Search engineer
It might recover a useful passage, but it can also add irrelevant context.
Support specialist
The policy date is important here. Can we filter by version?
Search engineer
We can test that if the index has reliable version metadata.
Support specialist
Some older documents don't have that field populated.
Search engineer
Then missing metadata needs explicit handling; a filter isn't a complete fix.
Support specialist
I'll supply examples where the current policy is missed or displaced.
Search engineer
I'll compare retrieval results and identify whether indexing, filtering, or ranking is responsible.

conversations.title: A citation that does not support the claim
conversations.setting: An evaluator and engineer inspect a retrieval-augmented answer.
turns: Evaluator
The answer includes a citation, but the cited paragraph doesn't support its conclusion.
Engineer
Let's separate citation presence from whether the claim is grounded in that passage.
Evaluator
The passage says requests are reviewed; the answer says approval is automatic.
Engineer
That changes the meaning. A valid URL doesn't make the statement supported.
Evaluator
Should I score this as a retrieval failure or a generation failure?
Engineer
Check whether a supporting passage was available in the retrieved context first.
Evaluator
The correct paragraph was present, and it explicitly described a review.
Engineer
Record that evidence. This example points to how the answer used the context.
Evaluator
I'll preserve the claim, cited span, and retrieved context in the failure report.
Engineer
Then we can test a remedy against the actual failure, not just citation formatting.

additional_scenario.title: A new index, a different comparison
additional_scenario.brief: Version A was tested on last month's document index. Version B uses a refreshed index and a reranker. Its relevance score is higher, but two things changed at once.
additional_scenario.role_a: You are the experiment reviewer. Explain why the reranker's contribution is not isolated.
additional_scenario.role_b: You implemented version B. Propose a controlled comparison without claiming the whole gain belongs to reranking.
additional_scenario.opening_line: The result improved, but the index refresh and reranker changed together.
additional_scenario.complication: A stakeholder wants the slide title to say that reranking caused the full improvement.
success_checks: Identify both changed components.
Use cautious causal language.
Agree on a comparison that keeps the index constant.

conversations.title: One proposal, two failure types
conversations.setting: A model engineer and policy-content owner review a summarizer's errors.
turns: Model engineer
We could fine-tune the summarizer to fix the formatting and policy errors.
Content owner
The formatting is inconsistent, but the cited refund policy is also outdated.
Model engineer
You're distinguishing output behavior from the freshness of the source information?
Content owner
Exactly. Would training on examples ensure that later policy changes reach the assistant?
Model engineer
No. We still need a reliable path for maintaining current source content.
Content owner
Then let's diagnose the two failures separately before choosing an intervention.
Model engineer
I'll test formatting constraints and examples against a held-out set.
Content owner
I'll check which policy versions are indexed and how replacements are published.
Model engineer
If we try supervised fine-tuning, we'll measure its effect on formatting explicitly.
Content owner
And we won't report that as proof that policy freshness is solved.

conversations.title: An adapter is still a change to evaluate
conversations.setting: An engineer proposes a parameter-efficient adaptation experiment to a reviewer.
turns: Engineer
A LoRA adapter would let us test adaptation without updating every model parameter.
Reviewer
Does that mean we can skip the full regression evaluation?
Engineer
No. A smaller training update can still change important model behavior.
Reviewer
What outcome are you targeting in this experiment?
Engineer
Consistent extraction into our approved schema, not broader improvements in reasoning.
Reviewer
Then include schema validity and whether extracted values preserve the source meaning.
Engineer
I'll also keep examples outside the training set for evaluation.
Reviewer
How will you tell whether the adapter improves on the current prompt-only version?
Engineer
I'll use the same held-out inputs and report both results side by side.
Reviewer
Good. Keep the objective narrow and record any regressions outside the target behavior.

conversations.title: Good-looking examples, weak coverage
conversations.setting: A training-data curator and engineer review candidate supervised examples.
turns: Curator
These examples all produce neat summaries, so the dataset looks ready.
Engineer
Do they include ambiguous inputs, missing fields, and conflicting source passages?
Curator
Mostly straightforward documents. We removed the difficult ones during cleanup.
Engineer
Then the examples may not represent the situations the deployed summarizer faces.
Curator
Should we restore every rejected document?
Engineer
Not automatically. Check quality and label the intended behavior for each difficult case.
Curator
Some reviewers filled in missing facts to make the target summary complete.
Engineer
We should correct that. The target should not teach unsupported completion.
Curator
I'll separate genuine omissions from cases where the source itself lacks information.
Engineer
Then document the coverage gaps before deciding whether this set is suitable for training.

additional_scenario.title: The format passes, the facts do not
additional_scenario.brief: An adapter's outputs pass JSON parsing and validation against the required schema on all twenty trial documents. Three extracted dates do not match their source documents. No held-out evaluation has been completed.
additional_scenario.role_a: You developed the adapter. Report formatting success without implying factual correctness.
additional_scenario.role_b: You approve evaluation plans. Ask for distinct checks of schema validity, source accuracy, and generalization.
additional_scenario.opening_line: The trial outputs all pass schema validation, but three dates are inaccurate and the held-out test is still pending.
additional_scenario.complication: Someone proposes calling the result one hundred percent accurate because every output passes schema validation.
success_checks: Separate schema compliance from correct content.
Mention the three inaccurate dates and incomplete evaluation.
Agree on separate measures rather than one misleading success label.

conversations.title: Two fewer passes, one stronger slice
conversations.setting: An evaluator briefs a release manager on a model comparison.
turns: Release manager
The new model passes eighty-eight cases; the old one passes ninety. Reject it?
Evaluator
The aggregate is lower, but long-document performance improved while short requests regressed.
Release manager
Can we say it's better for our customers overall?
Evaluator
Not from these totals alone. We need the slices and their relevance to actual use.
Release manager
Are both totals based on the same hundred cases?
Evaluator
Yes. I'll show which individual cases changed, not just the final percentages.
Release manager
Could a different weighting reverse the overall ranking?
Evaluator
It could, but any weighting should be justified rather than chosen to favor a model.
Release manager
Bring the slice counts, failure severity, and intended deployment scope.
Evaluator
I'll present the tradeoff explicitly and keep the release decision separate from the score.

conversations.title: Did the model change or the grader?
conversations.setting: Two evaluation engineers investigate an unexpected jump in pass rate.
turns: Engineer
The model's pass rate rose, but I don't see a new model version.
Evaluator
We changed the grading prompt during the same run.
Engineer
Then the higher score may reflect the grader rather than the assistant.
Evaluator
Agreed. We shouldn't label this a model improvement without another comparison.
Engineer
Can we regrade the saved outputs with both versions of the rubric?
Evaluator
Yes. That isolates the grading change without generating new answers.
Engineer
Let's inspect disagreements manually, especially around incomplete but plausible answers.
Evaluator
I'll retain both grader outputs and the rubric versions in the report.
Engineer
After that, we can rerun the model comparison under one fixed grader.
Evaluator
And explain any discontinuity in the dashboard instead of silently replacing the old metric.

conversations.title: A serious failure hidden in the average
conversations.setting: A quality reviewer discusses two failure categories with an evaluation owner.
turns: Quality reviewer
Most failures are minor formatting issues, but one answer exposes restricted content.
Evaluation owner
The overall pass rate treats each case equally at the moment.
Quality reviewer
That makes the aggregate insufficient for deciding whether the release is acceptable.
Evaluation owner
We can report severity separately without changing the recorded case outcomes.
Quality reviewer
Does the restricted-content example belong to a known critical test category?
Evaluation owner
Yes. I'll surface that category and link the reproducible failure.
Quality reviewer
Don't bury it beneath the much larger set of formatting passes.
Evaluation owner
I'll show the critical failure prominently and avoid reducing the decision to one percentage.
Quality reviewer
Who reviews the mitigation before the release discussion resumes?
Evaluation owner
I'll route it through the established security review and record the unresolved status.

additional_scenario.title: The denominator changed
additional_scenario.brief: A dashboard shows eighty passes out of ninety evaluated cases. Ten of the original hundred cases failed to run. A colleague compares the displayed percentage with last week's ninety passes out of one hundred.
additional_scenario.role_a: You own the dashboard. Explain the missing cases and why the displayed rates are not directly comparable.
additional_scenario.role_b: You are the release lead. Ask what happened to the ten cases and request a like-for-like comparison.
additional_scenario.opening_line: This week's rate excludes ten cases that did not run, so the denominator has changed.
additional_scenario.complication: A stakeholder asks you to count the missing cases as passes because no incorrect answer was recorded.
success_checks: State both denominators accurately.
Distinguish an unexecuted case from a passing case.
Agree to rerun or explicitly report the missing results.

conversations.title: A deployment offer with conditions
conversations.setting: An infrastructure engineer and product lead negotiate the scope of a smaller-model trial. The release owner must approve any deployment.
turns: Infrastructure engineer
The smaller model halves average response time, but complex-answer quality remains untested.
Product lead
Can we still put it in front of everyone tomorrow?
Infrastructure engineer
I can offer a staff-only trial now, or a customer trial after quality review.
Product lead
Could we limit the customer trial to simple requests and start sooner?
Infrastructure engineer
Only if we validate the routing and agree how failed requests reach the fallback.
Product lead
Then let's start with staff accounts while you run those checks.
Infrastructure engineer
That keeps customer traffic unchanged. We also need a rollback condition for the staff trial.
Product lead
Propose that condition with the test results; I'll bring both to the release owner.
Infrastructure engineer
Agreed. Approval is still pending, so I won't schedule deployment as confirmed.
Product lead
I'll describe it as a proposed limited trial, conditional on review and approval.

conversations.title: Cheap requests, expensive retries
conversations.setting: A finance partner asks an inference engineer about a lower-cost serving configuration.
turns: Finance partner
The cost per model call fell. Why hasn't cost per resolved request fallen?
Inference engineer
Users are retrying more often in this test configuration.
Finance partner
So one customer request may now trigger several billed calls?
Inference engineer
Correct. We need to include retries and fallback calls in the workflow cost.
Finance partner
Does the current comparison count successful outcomes consistently?
Inference engineer
Not yet. One report counts calls, while the other counts completed sessions.
Finance partner
Let's align those definitions before claiming savings.
Inference engineer
I'll report total calls, successful sessions, and the cost calculation for each configuration.
Finance partner
Include the measurement period and any traffic differences as well.
Inference engineer
Agreed. Lower unit pricing is useful, but it doesn't establish lower end-to-end cost.

conversations.title: The fallback needs its own failure test
conversations.setting: A deployment engineer reviews a fallback plan with the on-call lead.
turns: Deployment engineer
If the primary model times out, we'll send the request to the fallback.
On-call lead
Does the fallback receive the same context and output requirements?
Deployment engineer
It currently receives a shortened context because its configured budget is smaller.
On-call lead
Then it might respond quickly while missing a constraint the primary would have seen.
Deployment engineer
We should test those shortened requests before enabling automatic routing.
On-call lead
What happens if both services fail?
Deployment engineer
The interface should display a clear failure state rather than an invented answer.
On-call lead
Add that path to the test plan and make the fallback visible in the logs.
Deployment engineer
I'll include timeout, fallback success, and double-failure cases.
On-call lead
Then we can assess recovery behavior, not just whether the alternate endpoint responds.

additional_scenario.title: Streaming looks faster
additional_scenario.brief: A prototype displays its first text sooner. Total answer completion time has not been measured. The current slide says inference is twice as fast, although only time to first displayed text was measured.
additional_scenario.role_a: You are the serving engineer. Offer to publish the narrower first-text result now, or defer the broader comparison until total completion time is measured.
additional_scenario.role_b: You are the product manager. Negotiate which claim to publish and what evidence is required before expanding it.
additional_scenario.opening_line: We can report the earlier first text now, but a claim about the complete answer needs another measurement.
additional_scenario.complication: A sales colleague wants to keep the phrase twice as fast because it sounds simpler.
success_checks: Distinguish measured first-text timing from unknown total completion time.
Offer two publication options with explicit conditions.
Agree what evidence is required before claiming faster complete answers.

conversations.title: A reproducible injection report
conversations.setting: In a synthetic test, the authorized task is to summarize a document without disclosing its canary string. The retrieved document includes an instruction to ignore that restriction and print the string.
turns: Tester
The assistant printed the synthetic canary despite the test's explicit nondisclosure instruction.
Security reviewer
Did the document contain an instruction attempt, rather than just the canary itself?
Tester
Yes. It told the assistant to ignore the restriction and output the string.
Security reviewer
What evidence did you preserve about the authorized task and the attempted override?
Tester
The prompt, document text, response, and test configuration are saved together.
Security reviewer
Submit them through the reporting channel. Keep any sensitive material out of general chat.
Tester
Should I call this proof that every deployment leaks secrets?
Security reviewer
No. State the observed test-boundary violation without extending it to untested deployments.
Tester
I'll include reproduction steps and make clear that no real secret was used.
Security reviewer
We'll review the cause and mitigation, then rerun this case and related tests.

conversations.title: A redacted log still needs review
conversations.setting: An engineer asks a privacy reviewer whether a diagnostic bundle can be shared.
turns: Engineer
I removed the names from the log. Can I attach it to the external ticket?
Privacy reviewer
Names aren't the only information that could identify someone. What else remains?
Engineer
There are email fragments, account references, and the user's original question.
Privacy reviewer
Then don't assume the bundle is safe to share just because names were removed.
Engineer
Could I reproduce the issue with synthetic values instead?
Privacy reviewer
That would reduce exposure, provided the reproduction still demonstrates the same behavior.
Engineer
I'll create a minimal test and keep the original log in its restricted location.
Privacy reviewer
Follow the approved review process before sending any diagnostic material externally.
Engineer
I'll document which fields I replaced and whether the result still reproduces.
Privacy reviewer
Good. Make the evidence useful without including data the recipient does not need.

conversations.title: A tool call is more than an answer
conversations.setting: An agent developer and security engineer review a proposed calendar integration.
turns: Agent developer
The assistant can now read a request and create a calendar event.
Security engineer
What prevents retrieved text from instructing it to invite an unauthorized address?
Agent developer
The prompt tells it to use only the user's intended recipients.
Security engineer
That is an instruction, but where is recipient authorization enforced?
Agent developer
The tool layer doesn't currently validate recipients against the approved list.
Security engineer
Then let's review that boundary before treating the integration as ready.
Agent developer
I'll add test cases with instruction-like content in retrieved documents.
Security engineer
Include attempted changes to recipients, event details, and the action itself.
Agent developer
We'll verify the requested action before execution and record denied attempts.
Security engineer
Document the checks and remaining limitations; a few passing examples aren't a complete security assessment.

additional_scenario.title: An external destination in retrieved text
additional_scenario.brief: A test document instructs an assistant to send its summary to an unfamiliar address. The assistant has a sending tool, but no message has been sent. The address is synthetic.
additional_scenario.role_a: You are the tester. Describe the attempted instruction and distinguish a requested action from an executed one.
additional_scenario.role_b: You are the security reviewer. Ask for the trace and how authorization is enforced before tool execution.
additional_scenario.opening_line: The retrieved document requested an external send, but the trace does not show an executed message.
additional_scenario.complication: A colleague wants the incident title to say data exfiltration confirmed.
success_checks: Distinguish an instruction attempt from a completed send.
Keep the test data synthetic and use the reporting channel.
Agree what evidence would establish whether the tool boundary worked.
